title: mmHg, kPa, cmH₂O: The Three Pressure Units Every Clinician Toggles
h1: Clinical pressure units — mmHg, kPa and cmH₂O
description: Arterial pressure in mmHg, CVP in cmH₂O, ventilator settings in cmH₂O or kPa. Sloppy conversions misset PEEP by 40%.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: 1 mmHg = 0.1333 kPa = 1.36 cmH₂O. A 120 mmHg BP is 16.0 kPa. A 10 cmH₂O PEEP is 7.35 mmHg.
body: Clinical medicine runs on three pressure units simultaneously. The unit each device uses is not chosen for arithmetic convenience — it is historical. Fluency between them is a patient safety issue.

> 1 mmHg = 0.13332 kPa = 1.3595 cmH₂O
> 1 kPa = 7.5006 mmHg = 10.197 cmH₂O
> 1 cmH₂O = 0.09806 kPa = 0.7356 mmHg

mmHg: arterial and venous pressures, intraocular pressure, intracranial pressure. cmH₂O: airway pressures, PEEP, CPAP, CVP by water manometer. kPa: European ventilators, arterial blood gas partial pressures, some ICU monitors.

Ventilator PEEP prescribed at 10 cmH₂O = 7.4 mmHg = 0.98 kPa. If a device configured in mmHg is set to 10 (thinking cmH₂O), it delivers 13.6 cmH₂O — 36% above prescription and enough to trigger barotrauma in ARDS patients.
Airway → cmH₂O. Blood → mmHg. Europe → kPa. Convert before you compare.

faqs.q: Why does BP still use mmHg?
faqs.a: Historical continuity — mercury sphygmomanometers set the reference and modern devices report the same units to preserve interoperability with clinical guidelines.

faqs.q: Is torr the same as mmHg?
faqs.a: To six figures, yes. Modern SI-strict practice prefers torr because mmHg depends on mercury density and local gravity.
